The book is a Greek narrative covering the same ground as 2 Chronicles 35-36, Ezra, and Nehemiah 7:73-8:12, and its Greek runs free and idiomatic where the Greek of Ezra-Nehemiah runs stiff and literal, the mark of a translator working from Hebrew and Aramaic sources rather than a writer composing in Greek. The text was complete by AD 93 or 94, when Josephus followed 1 Esdras instead of the Greek Ezra-Nehemiah through Antiquities of the Jews 11.1-158 and treated it as Scripture. Augustine took up the book in City of God 18.36 (c. AD 426), reading the third young man's verdict that truth is strongest of all as pointing to Christ, who is the Truth.

The narrative runs from Josiah's Passover to Ezra's reading of the Law. Chapter 1 parallels 2 Chronicles 35:1-36:21: the Passover kept in Josiah's eighteenth year (1:20), his death from wounds taken against Pharaoh at Megiddo, the burning of the temple, and the seventy years of sabbath for the land. Chapter 2 carries Cyrus's decree and the vessels sent through the treasurer Mithridates to Sheshbazzar (Ezra 1), then the letters of Rehum and the scribe Shimshai to Artaxerxes that halt the work (Ezra 4:7-24). From 5:7 through 7:15 the book parallels Ezra 2:1-6:22: the register of returning exiles, the Festival of Booths, the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah, the scroll of Cyrus found in the archives at Ecbatana, and the house finished on the twenty-third of Adar in the sixth year of Darius (7:5). Chapters 8:1-9:36 parallel Ezra 7-10, Ezra's journey up from Babylon in the seventh year of Artaxerxes (8:6) and the matter of the foreign wives. Then 9:37-55 parallels Nehemiah 7:73-8:12, where Ezra reads the law from a wooden platform and the Levites explain it. The book breaks off in the middle of that account at 9:55 and does not continue into Nehemiah 8:13. One long section has no Hebrew parallel anywhere: the contest of the three bodyguards of Darius (3:1-5:6). Each man seals his answer to what is strongest under the sleeping king's pillow. The first says wine, the second says the king, and the third, Zerubbabel, argues for women and then names truth greatest of all, and the assembly shouts, "Great is truth and strongest of all!" (4:41). Offered anything he asks, Zerubbabel asks Darius to keep the vow he made on the day he became king, to rebuild Jerusalem and send back its vessels (4:43-46). The order of the material also differs from Ezra. Read straight through, 1 Esdras puts the Artaxerxes correspondence (2:15-30) before the reign of Darius rather than after it as at Ezra 4:7-24, and it puts the contest and the royal grant before the register of returning exiles rather than immediately after Cyrus's decree. The arrangement is built around the contest, which sits at the center with the return running out from it on both sides.

The events span roughly 622 to 458 BC. Josiah's Passover falls in 622 BC, while Assyria collapses and Pharaoh Neco marches to the Euphrates; Josiah dies at Megiddo in 609 BC. Jerusalem falls to Nebuchadnezzar and the temple burns in 586 BC. Cyrus takes Babylon and issues his decree in 538 BC, the temple is finished in the sixth year of Darius I in 516 BC, and Ezra comes up in the seventh year of Artaxerxes I in 458 BC. The whole return happens inside the Achaemenid Persian empire.

The names are the hardest part of this book. Esdras is the Greek and Latin form of the Hebrew Ezra (עֶזְרָא), meaning "help." In the Septuagint this book is Esdras A (Ἔσδρας Αʹ), and it stands before Esdras B (Ἔσδρας Βʹ), which is Ezra and Nehemiah together as a single book. Latin manuscripts and the Vulgate call it 3 Esdras, counting Ezra as the first book and Nehemiah as the second. The Slavonic Bible calls it 2 Ezra. English Bibles that print it call it 1 Esdras, following the Greek. It is received in the Eastern Orthodox canon and stands in Greek Bibles as Esdras A. Jerome judged the third and fourth books of Ezra apocryphal in his prologue to Ezra (c. AD 394) and translated only the Hebrew Ezra-Nehemiah. The Council of Trent (Session IV, 8 April 1546) did not list it among the canonical books; the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate, printed 9 November 1592, placed 3 Esdras, 4 Esdras, and the Prayer of Manasseh in an appendix after the New Testament, expressly outside the series of canonical books (extra seriem canonicorum librorum). The King James Bible of 1611 printed it among the Apocrypha as 1 Esdras.
